notes.text: An EKS Auto Mode cluster: Auto Mode runs Karpenter for us. Only its built-in NodePools exist; the system pool's nodes run the cluster add-ons.

Every label Auto Mode lets a NodePool select on: family, size, vCPUs, memory, generation, GPUs. The closest to speed is the vendor's clock rate. Nothing on measured performance, caches, or what a unit of performance costs; and Karpenter launches the cheapest allowed type.
The controller from the v0.1.1 release. It runs on Auto Mode's general-purpose pool and reads the public Spare Cores API: specs, prices and benchmark results of every instance type.

GILty is a Python app held back by the GIL: it learns Moby-Dick as a Markov chain and babbles in its style, one dependent hash lookup after the other, so only a faster core and cache make it faster. The team picked r5a.large for it by hand ("memory-optimized, for Python"): a plain Karpenter NodePool pinned to that type.
Auto Mode launches the r5a.large. Time-lapse.
Its speed, every five seconds, in real time: the instance type and CPU, then words per second, then a sample of the babble.

Same size, same budget, measured data: at least the r5a.large's 2 vCPUs and 16 GiB, for at most 10% more ($0.1392/h, Auto Mode fee included); instance families ranked by PassMark's single-threaded score, the benchmark that tracks GILty best, keeping those within 10% of the fastest. No Karpenter label can say any of this.
The controller generated a plain Karpenter NodePool with the instance types that qualify.
A second, identical GILty, on the pool Spare Cores picked. The first one keeps running on its r5a.large.
Both copies, live, every five seconds: the same program on the hand-picked r5a.large and on the instance Spare Cores picked. Each line starts with the instance type and the CPU.
